subject: biology-hl
author: original (NevaIB)
title: Nucleic acids
bigPicture: DNA and RNA are polymers of nucleotides. A strong sugar–phosphate backbone carries a variable sequence of bases, and complementary base pairing lets that sequence be copied and read.

keyIdeas.cue: What is the genetic material of all living organisms?
keyIdeas.answer: DNA. Some viruses use RNA, but viruses are not considered living.

keyIdeas.cue: What are the parts of a nucleotide and how are they drawn?
keyIdeas.answer: A phosphate (circle), a pentose sugar (pentagon) and a nitrogenous base (rectangle). The phosphate attaches to one side of the sugar and the base to another.
Covalent bonds between the phosphate of one nucleotide and the sugar of the next make a continuous, strong sugar–phosphate chain. The bases stick out from it.
DNA: adenine, thymine, guanine, cytosine. RNA: adenine, uracil, guanine, cytosine.
Nucleotides are linked by condensation into a single strand. You should be able to draw a short RNA chain.
Two antiparallel strands held together by hydrogen bonds between complementary bases: A with T and G with C, twisted into a double helix. You don't need to draw the helix.

keyIdeas.cue: Three differences between DNA and RNA.
keyIdeas.answer: DNA has two strands, RNA usually one. DNA has thymine, RNA has uracil. DNA has deoxyribose (no –OH on carbon 2), RNA has ribose (–OH on carbon 2).

keyIdeas.cue: Why does complementary base pairing matter?
keyIdeas.answer: It is based on hydrogen bonding, and each base can pair with only one partner, so each strand is a template. This allows accurate replication (DNA to DNA) and expression (DNA to mRNA to protein).

keyIdeas.cue: Why can DNA store limitless information?
keyIdeas.answer: Any base can follow any other, and molecules can be any length, so the number of possible sequences is 4ⁿ for n bases. A huge amount of information fits in a tiny volume.

keyIdeas.cue: Why is the shared genetic code evidence for common ancestry?
keyIdeas.answer: Almost all organisms use the same codons for the same amino acids. This is best explained by descent from a common ancestor, not by independent origins.

keyIdeas.cue: What does 5′→3′ directionality mean and why does it matter?
keyIdeas.answer: Each strand has a 5′ end (phosphate) and a 3′ end (sugar –OH). Nucleotides are only added to the 3′ end, so replication, transcription and translation all have a direction, and the two DNA strands run in opposite directions.

keyIdeas.cue: Why does purine–pyrimidine pairing stabilise the helix?
keyIdeas.answer: A purine (A or G, two rings) always pairs with a pyrimidine (T or C, one ring). A–T and G–C pairs are the same width, so the helix has a constant diameter whatever the sequence.
DNA wrapped around a core of eight histone proteins, with one further histone attached to the linker DNA that holds it in place. Molecular visualisation software is used to study it.

keyIdeas.cue: How did Hershey and Chase show DNA is the genetic material?
keyIdeas.answer: Bacteriophages were labelled with ³⁵S (in protein, not DNA) or ³²P (in DNA, not protein), then allowed to infect bacteria, which were then shaken and centrifuged. ³²P ended up in the bacterial pellet and ³⁵S in the liquid, so DNA, not protein, entered the cells. It only became possible once radioisotopes were available.

In every species tested, A ≈ T and G ≈ C, but the proportions differed between species. This falsified the tetranucleotide hypothesis, which predicted equal amounts of all four bases in a repeating unit. It is an example of falsification answering the problem of induction.

keyIdeas.cue: Which carbons of the pentose carry the base and the phosphate?
keyIdeas.answer: Number the sugar's carbons 1′–5′. The base joins at C1′, the phosphate at C5′, and the next nucleotide's phosphate links to C3′. That is why strands have a 5′ end and a 3′ end.

keyIdeas.cue: Name some types of nucleic acid you should recognise.
keyIdeas.answer: DNA in the nucleus, plus the small circular DNA in mitochondria and chloroplasts; RNA as mRNA (message), tRNA (carries amino acids) and rRNA (part of ribosomes). Certain viruses carry their genes as RNA rather than DNA.

keyTerms.def: Monomer of nucleic acids: phosphate + pentose + base.
The two strands run in opposite 5′→3′ directions.
A–T (A–U in RNA) and G–C, held by hydrogen bonds.
DNA wound around a histone octamer.

workedExamples.title: Use Chargaff's rule
workedExamples.prompt: A DNA sample has 30% adenine. Deduce the percentages of T, G and C.

misconceptions.wrong: The backbone is held by hydrogen bonds.
misconceptions.right: The backbone is covalent. Hydrogen bonds join the two strands.

misconceptions.wrong: A pairs with U in DNA.
misconceptions.right: A pairs with T in DNA. U replaces T only in RNA.

misconceptions.wrong: Viruses prove some living things use RNA as genetic material.
misconceptions.right: Viruses aren't considered living. All living organisms use DNA.

misconceptions.wrong: Chargaff showed all four bases are equal.
misconceptions.right: He showed A = T and G = C, with ratios varying between species.

misconceptions.wrong: Both DNA strands can be drawn running the same way.
misconceptions.right: Draw them antiparallel: label 5′ and 3′ at each end, with one strand upside down relative to the other.
